title: Lateral Medullary Syndrome and Cranial Nerve Palsies

steps.tx: Infarction of the posterolateral medulla due to thromboembolic occlusion of the intracranial vertebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) produces **Wallenberg syndrome**. In sharp contrast to medial medullary stroke, lateral medullary infarction selectively spares the descending corticospinal motor pyramids, preserving limb strength while destroying multiple sensory nuclei, sympathetic pathways, and lower cranial nerve connections.
steps.say: Infarction of the posterolateral medulla due to occlusion of the vertebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery produces Wallenberg syndrome. Lateral medullary infarction selectively spares the descending motor pyramids, preserving limb strength while destroying sensory nuclei, descending sympathetics, and cranial nerve connections.

steps.tx: The sensory signature of lateral medullary syndrome is a striking dissociated, crossed sensory deficit. Ischaemic injury to the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract abolishes pain and temperature sensation across the ipsilateral hemiface. Simultaneously, damage to the traversing spinothalamic tract causes loss of pain and temperature sensation over the contralateral trunk and limbs, confirming an alternating **crossed sensory loss**.
steps.say: The sensory signature of lateral medullary syndrome is a striking dissociated crossed sensory deficit. Injury to the spinal trigeminal tract abolishes pain and temperature over the ipsilateral face. Simultaneously, destruction of the spinothalamic tract causes loss of pain and temperature over the contralateral body.

steps.tx: Motor innervation of the larynx, pharynx, and upper palate originates within the specialised lower motor neuron pool termed the **nucleus ambiguus**. In lateral medullary infarction, ischaemic injury to this nucleus impairs ninth and tenth cranial nerve efferents, causing acute palatal droop with uvular deviation away from the lesion, intractable dysphagia, nasal regurgitation of fluids, and prominent hoarse dysphonia.
steps.say: Motor innervation of the larynx, pharynx, and palate originates within the specialized lower motor neuron pool termed the nucleus ambiguus. In lateral medullary infarction, injury to this nucleus impairs cranial nerves nine and ten, causing acute palatal droop, intractable dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, and hoarse dysphonia.

steps.tx: Interruption of descending first-order sympathetic axons travelling through the dorsolateral brainstem tegmentum produces an ipsilateral **Horner syndrome**. Clinical signs include mild upper eyelid ptosis from denervation of the superior tarsal muscle, pupillary miosis that is more pronounced in dim illumination, and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis with cutaneous flushing resulting from loss of sympathetic sudomotor tone.
steps.say: Interruption of descending sympathetic axons travelling through the dorsolateral brainstem produces an ipsilateral Horner syndrome. Clinical signs include mild upper eyelid ptosis, pupillary miosis more pronounced in dim light, and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis with cutaneous flushing from loss of sympathetic tone.

steps.tx: Peripheral dysfunction of cranial nerves in the brainstem or periphery presents with specific deficits based on their anatomical course. A complete **third nerve palsy** manifests with ptosis, an eye resting down and out, and an unreactive dilated pupil when parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres are compressed by an expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm, requiring immediate emergency vascular neuroimaging.

steps.tx: An acute, idiopathic peripheral lower motor neuron paralysis of the seventh cranial nerve is universally designated as **Bell palsy**. Patients present with abrupt unilateral facial weakness involving all muscle groups on that side. Critical physical signs include inability to wrinkle the ipsilateral forehead, failure of complete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos), upward globe rotation upon attempted closure (Bell phenomenon), and angle of mouth drooping.
steps.say: An acute idiopathic peripheral lower motor neuron paralysis of the seventh cranial nerve is designated as Bell palsy. Patients present with abrupt unilateral facial weakness involving all muscle groups on that side. Critical signs include inability to wrinkle the forehead, incomplete eyelid closure, and drooping of the mouth angle.

vis.alt: Physical examination and clinical signs of facial nerve palsy.
vis.caption: Examination of facial nerve motor branches and peripheral Bell palsy signs. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The fundamental neurological distinction in facial weakness rests on distinguishing upper from lower motor neuron distribution. Upper motor neuron lesions (such as hemispheric cortical stroke) spare the forehead due to bilateral corticobulbar innervation of the upper facial nucleus. Conversely, lower motor neuron lesions like Bell palsy paralyse the entire ipsilateral hemiface, including the **frontalis** muscle, causing total loss of forehead furrowing.

steps.tx: Therapeutic management of acute Bell palsy mandates early intervention with a seven-day course of high-dose oral **prednisolone** initiated within seventy-two hours of symptom onset to reduce perineural oedema within the rigid facial canal. Adjunctive corneal lubrication with artificial tears and nighttime eye taping is mandatory to prevent exposure keratitis, corneal ulceration, and permanent visual loss from incomplete blinking.
steps.say: Therapeutic management of acute Bell palsy mandates early intervention with high-dose oral prednisolone started within seventy-two hours of symptom onset to reduce edema within the facial canal. Aggressive corneal lubrication and nighttime eye taping are essential to prevent exposure keratitis and corneal ulceration.
